perspective:
From Carolyn Abebe’s available perspective:

- I am Carolyn Abebe, a Black woman, a bank teller with a bachelor’s degree.
- Marilyn Olson is my colleague at the community bank; she is a white woman and a sales representative. We recently started working together and are still getting to know each other; I perceive mutual professional respect.
- During a busy week with increased customer traffic and stress, I noticed Marilyn had been unusually quiet and withdrawn for several days, unlike her normally engaging demeanor. I asked if everything was alright and if she wanted to talk. She told me she was overwhelmed with work and some personal stuff, and thanked me.
- Later, Marilyn was curt with me in an interaction. I felt confused and slightly hurt. I told her I hoped I hadn’t overstepped, that I’d had tough times too, and that talking sometimes helps. She said she appreciated it, apologized if she seemed off, and said it had been a hard week.
- After that, Marilyn appeared to respond positively to my openness. I felt relieved and hopeful. I invited her to a small get-together with friends that weekend. She said it sounded lovely, thanked me, and accepted.
- Despite friendly interactions outside work, I felt Marilyn was still maintaining a professional distance at the bank, and I felt disappointed. I asked to talk about our work dynamic and said I felt a distance I couldn’t understand. She said she didn’t realize it, apologized if it seemed that way, and agreed we should talk to improve collaboration.
- After our private meeting, I believed we had cleared the air and better understood each other’s professional expectations and personal boundaries. I felt content and optimistic. I proposed teaming up on the new project proposal. She agreed, said she was glad we had the talk, and looked forward to working more closely with me.

I do not have access to Marilyn’s private thoughts, exact personal troubles, hidden reasons, or any information she did not tell or show me.
